That is a clue that Triton was not born there: it was probably caught by Neptune’s gravity long ago. Triton is one of the coldest places ever measured, and it has geysers that blow out dark dust. Very, very slowly, Triton is moving closer to Neptune.
description.standard: Triton is by far Neptune’s largest moon, 2,707 km across and a little bigger than the dwarf planet Pluto. It orbits Neptune backwards – against the planet’s rotation – and is the only large moon in the solar system to do so, which is why astronomers think Neptune captured it from the Kuiper belt long ago. When Voyager 2 flew past in 1989, it saw geysers of nitrogen gas carrying dark dust about 8 km high, on a surface at about −235 °C. Tides are slowly pulling Triton inward, so in billions of years it may be torn apart into rings or fall into Neptune.
description.advanced: Triton’s orbit is retrograde and tilted about 157° to Neptune’s equator, which cannot be explained by formation in a disk around the planet; the leading explanation is the capture of a Kuiper belt object, perhaps one member of a binary pair whose partner was thrown away. Capture would have left Triton on a highly eccentric orbit, and damping that orbit to today’s near-perfect circle (e ≈ 0.00002) may have melted its interior and scattered or destroyed Neptune’s original moons. Its surface of nitrogen, methane and water ice reflects most of the sunlight it receives (albedo about 0.76), which helps keep it at about 38 K. Because it orbits against Neptune’s rotation, the tidal bulge it raises slowly drains its orbital energy; it may reach Neptune’s Roche limit in several billion years, although estimates range from about 3.6 to 28 billion years.

simple: Triton was found in 1846, only 17 days after Neptune itself was discovered.
Triton is so icy and bright that it reflects most of the sunlight that reaches it.
Only one spacecraft has ever visited Triton: Voyager 2, in 1989.
standard: Triton contains more than 99.5 % of all the mass orbiting Neptune.
Parts of Triton’s surface are wrinkled into a pattern called cantaloupe terrain, because it looks like the skin of a melon.
Triton takes 5.9 days to orbit Neptune and always keeps the same face towards it, just as our Moon does with Earth.
advanced: Triton has a very thin nitrogen atmosphere with a surface pressure of about 1.4 Pa, roughly 1/70,000 of Earth’s.
Some models suggest that heat from radioactive decay and tides could keep a liquid ocean beneath Triton’s icy crust.
Surface gravity is 0.78 m/s², about 8 % of Earth’s.

simple: Triton is about 150 degrees colder than the coldest temperature ever measured on Earth.
standard: Triton circles Neptune the wrong way round, like a car driving backwards around a roundabout – a clue that Neptune captured it from the Kuiper belt.
advanced: Triton is about 14 % wider than Pluto, with a similar density and similar nitrogen, methane and water ices – a Pluto-like world that Neptune took for itself.

description.simple: Nereid is a small, grey moon of Neptune. Its path around Neptune is not a circle but a long, stretched oval. Sometimes it comes quite close to Neptune, and then it swings far out again. Scientists think something big may have thrown it onto this strange path long ago.
description.standard: Nereid is about 340 km across and has one of the most stretched-out orbits of any known moon. During its 360-day orbit, its distance from Neptune swings from about 1.4 million km to about 9.7 million km – nearly seven times farther. Gerard Kuiper discovered it in 1949; it was the second moon of Neptune ever found and the last one discovered before Voyager 2 arrived in 1989. Astronomers long thought Nereid was a captured object, but a 2026 study suggests it may be one of Neptune’s original moons, flung onto its wild orbit when Triton arrived.
description.advanced: Nereid’s orbit has an eccentricity of about 0.75, one of the highest known for any moon, with its closest point near 1.37 million km and its farthest near 9.65 million km from Neptune. It is prograde and only modestly inclined, unlike typical irregular moons, which are thought to be captured bodies. Two origins have been proposed: a captured Kuiper belt object, or a regular moon of Neptune scattered outward when Triton was captured. In 2026, James Webb Space Telescope spectra showed crystalline water ice and carbon dioxide and a surface unlike Kuiper belt objects but similar to the moons of Uranus, favouring the second idea – if so, Nereid may be the last intact survivor of Neptune’s original family of moons.

simple: Nereid was discovered in 1949 by an astronomer called Gerard Kuiper.
Nereid is Neptune’s third-biggest moon.
Nobody has ever seen a close-up picture of Nereid.
standard: Voyager 2 could only photograph Nereid from about 4.7 million km away, so its shape and surface are still largely unknown.
Nereid spins once in about 11.6 hours, as measured with the Kepler space telescope.
The small outer moon Halimede has a similar grey colour and may be a fragment knocked off Nereid in a collision.
advanced: Nereid’s mean diameter is about 340 km, similar to that of Saturn’s moon Mimas.
Nereid is by far the largest of Neptune’s irregular moons, holding about 98 % of their combined mass (not counting Triton).
Nereid’s brightness has been seen to vary strongly over days to years, and the cause is still not fully explained.

simple: Nereid takes almost exactly as long to go around Neptune as Earth takes to go around the Sun.
standard: Nereid swings in toward Neptune and back out again like a comet – at its farthest it is about seven times as far away as at its closest.
advanced: Even at its closest, Nereid is about 3.6 times as far from Neptune as our Moon is from Earth; at its farthest, it is about 25 times as far.

description.simple: Proteus is a dark, lumpy moon of Neptune, about 420 km wide. It is almost big enough for its own gravity to squeeze it into a ball – but not quite, so it looks like a dented box. Even though it is quite big, nobody saw it until the space probe Voyager 2 flew past Neptune in 1989. It had been hiding in Neptune’s bright glow.
description.standard: Proteus is Neptune’s second-largest moon, about 420 km across, yet it was only discovered in 1989 in images from Voyager 2. From Earth it is lost in the glare of Neptune, because it orbits only about 117,600 km from the planet’s centre – less than five Neptune radii – and its surface reflects only about a tenth of the sunlight that falls on it. Proteus is about as big as a body like it can get without its own gravity pulling it into a round shape, so it remains an irregular, box-like lump. It races around Neptune in just 27 hours.
description.advanced: With a mean diameter of about 420 km, Proteus is close to the size at which self-gravity should overcome the strength of ice and rock and pull a body into a roughly spheroidal (hydrostatic) shape – yet it has stayed irregular. Its surface is dominated by the impact basin Pharos, about 255 km wide and 10–15 km deep, made by an impact that nearly shattered the moon. Scientists think Proteus did not form together with Neptune but re-accreted from debris after Neptune captured Triton, whose arrival would have disrupted the original moon system. The tiny moon Hippocamp, found in Hubble images in 2013, orbits only about 12,000 km inside Proteus’s orbit and may be a fragment knocked off by the Pharos impact.

simple: Proteus goes around Neptune in a little more than one day.
From Proteus, Neptune would look about 50 times as wide as the full Moon looks to us.
Proteus has a giant crater that is more than half as wide as the whole moon.
standard: Voyager 2 found Proteus in 1989, a few weeks before flying past Neptune.
Proteus is named after a shape-changing sea god of Greek myths – fitting for such an oddly shaped moon.
Triton, Neptune’s largest moon, is more than six times as wide as Proteus.
advanced: Proteus orbits more slowly (26.9 h) than Neptune rotates (about 16.1 h), so tides are slowly pushing it outward.
Proteus’s mass has never been measured precisely, so its density and surface gravity (probably around 0.07 m/s²) are still uncertain.
Its nearly circular orbit close to Neptune’s equatorial plane is typical of a moon born in a disc around the planet – unlike the orbits of Triton and Nereid.

simple: Driving across Proteus on a motorway would take about four hours.
standard: Proteus is bigger than Nereid, which astronomers spotted from Earth in 1949, yet Proteus stayed hidden for another 40 years – a lump of coal sitting next to a floodlight.
advanced: Saturn’s moon Mimas, about 396 km across, is round, while the slightly larger Proteus is not – the size at which a moon becomes round depends on what it is made of and how warm it once was.
